analysis.one_liner: Bans the manufacture and sale of semiautomatic assault weapons and large-capacity ammunition magazines.
analysis.headline: The bill sat in the Senate Judiciary Committee without a hearing or vote for the entire two-year Congress and died in January 2023 with 41 cosponsors and no Republican support.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it a federal crime to import, sell, manufacture, transfer, or possess certain semiautomatic rifles, pistols, and shotguns — the kinds named in a long list of specific models like AR-15s and AK-47s — along with ammunition magazines holding more than 10 rounds. Weapons already legally owned would be 'grandfathered': owners could keep them, and dealers could still sell them with a background check. It also funds local gun buy-back programs and requires date markings on new weapons. The bill never moved past its referral to the Judiciary Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: The public, in the form of reduced availability of the semiautomatic rifles and large-capacity magazines that have been used in many high-casualty mass shootings. First responders and police are exempt from the ban, as are traditional hunting rifles, bolt- and lever-action guns, antiques, and roughly 2,000 models specifically listed as exempt in the bill's appendix. Current owners keep their guns.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it a federal crime to import, sell, manufacture, transfer, or possess semiautomatic assault weapons and large-capacity ammunition feeding devices, with exceptions for law enforcement, nuclear-materials security, retired officers, and authorized testing [S2].

Grandfathers weapons already lawfully owned: owners may keep them, and grandfathered semiautomatic assault weapons may still be sold or transferred after a licensed dealer runs a background check; owners must store them securely away from anyone legally barred from having a gun [S2][S3].
Lets state and local governments use federal Edward Byrne Memorial grant money to pay individuals who surrender a banned weapon or large-capacity magazine under a buy-back program [S2].

Requires newly manufactured assault weapons and large-capacity magazines to carry serial numbers and dates of manufacture, and directs the Attorney General to keep and publish a public record of crimes committed with these weapons [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Firearm manufacturers and dealers lose a large legal market: the bill names hundreds of specific AR-15, AK-pattern, and other semiautomatic models that could no longer be made or sold new, and it bans future production of magazines holding more than 10 rounds. Existing gun owners keep their weapons but face new storage requirements and background checks when selling grandfathered guns, and large-capacity magazines they own could no longer be resold.
analysis.who_pays_short: Firearm makers, dealers, and gun owners

drawbacks.text: The grandfather clause means millions of semiautomatic assault weapons and large-capacity magazines already in private hands would remain in circulation; the bill stops future sales but does not remove existing weapons, so any effect on availability would be gradual [S2].

The definition covers weapons by design features such as pistol grips, threaded barrels, and barrel shrouds, as well as a model-by-model list; opponents argue this sweeps in widely owned firearms and that the previous 1994-2004 federal assault weapons ban produced no clear reduction in overall gun homicides — a fair objection, since studies of that ban were inconclusive about its effect on total firearm violence even while it appears to have reduced use of the banned guns in crimes.

Long guns, including semiautomatic rifles, account for a minority of U.S. gun homicides, which are committed mostly with handguns; supporters respond that the bill targets the weapons used in mass shootings, but the broader public-safety benefit is smaller than the headline suggests.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The honest case is that the bill cuts off future sales of the specific weapon class used in the deadliest mass shootings while leaving current owners alone and exempting conventional hunting firearms. The honest cost is that it restricts a category of firearms millions of Americans own and value, that grandfathering blunts any near-term effect, and that the evidence from the earlier 1994 ban on overall homicide rates is inconclusive. Whether the trade is worth it depends heavily on how much weight one puts on preventing mass-shooting casualties versus restricting a popular civilian firearm — but the bill never got far enough for that debate to happen on the floor.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in March 2021 and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never took it up; the bill died when the Congress ended in January 2023 without a hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Senator Dianne Feinstein introduced the bill on March 11, 2021, with 34 original cosponsors including Majority Leader Chuck Schumer [S3].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Judiciary Committee the same day; no further action appears in its record [S5].
It finished with 41 cosponsors — 39 of 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of 2 Senate Independents — and no Republican cosponsor [S4].

The bill would have criminalized importing, selling, manufacturing, transferring, or possessing semiautomatic assault weapons and magazines holding more than 10 rounds, while grandfathering existing weapons and exempting law enforcement, retired officers, and roughly 2,000 specifically listed firearm models [S2][S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearm manufacturers and dealers who sell semiautomatic rifles and large-capacity magazines kept their market untouched, and gun owners faced no new restrictions. The status quo — in which these weapons remain freely manufactured and sold — prevailed by default because the committee never acted.

for.name: Dianne Feinstein
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 40 cosponsors across the Democratic caucus.

against.name: Richard Durbin
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee to which the bill was referred; the committee held no hearing or markup and the bill never advanced [S5]. Durbin was himself a cosponsor [S4].

against.name: 50 of 50 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: No Republican cosponsored the bill [S4], and with 50 seats the party had the numbers to block any assault weapons ban from reaching 60 votes on the floor.

against.name: National Rifle Association
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against federal assault weapons bans during this period, as it has consistently opposed restrictions on semiautomatic rifles and large-capacity magazines.

sides.party_line_note: All 41 cosponsors were Democrats or the Senate's Independent — 39 of 48 Democrats and 1 of 2 Independents — with zero of 50 Republicans signing on, and the bill died in a Democratic-led committee without a vote [S4].

industries.note: The bill bans new manufacture and sale of a long list of AR-15, AK-pattern, and similar semiautomatic models, closing one of the industry's largest and fastest-growing product lines. Manufacturers benefit from the bill's failure, which keeps the market open.
New production of magazines holding more than 10 rounds would become unlawful, ending sales of large-capacity magazines to civilians.

Dealers would lose the banned weapons as sellable inventory and would have to run background checks on private-party sales of grandfathered assault weapons, adding cost and friction to a legal channel.
The bill's central premise — that Second Amendment rights are 'not unlimited' — runs directly against these groups' advocacy position; its failure preserves their policy framework.
